scenes.narration: Two services that get bundled together in casual conversation, and pulled apart mercilessly on the exam. CloudFront caches content at edge locations for speed. Route 53 — the name is a nod to port fifty three, the standard D N S port — routes queries and health-checks endpoints for resilience and compliance. This chapter sits inside two exam domains at once: Design High-Performing Architectures, twenty four percent of the associate exam, and Design Resilient Architectures, twenty six percent. The two services only add up to a real disaster-recovery story when you deliberately wire origin failover and D N S failover together — neither one covers the other by accident.

facts.label: CloudFront
facts.value: Edge caching for speed — not a substitute for origin failover

facts.label: Route 53
facts.value: DNS routing + health checks — six policies, one real job each

scenes.narration: Here's the trap. A scenario asks for a highly available global app, and the tempting move is to drop CloudFront in front of a single origin and call availability solved — because a globally distributed edge network sounds resilient. A second, quieter mistake: whenever a scenario says "route by location" or "gradually roll out a new version," candidates default to Simple routing because it's first on the list and sounds safe. Neither instinct survives contact with how these services actually work.

props.heading: "Put CloudFront in front of it and it's resilient now"
bullets: Add CloudFront to a single-origin app and consider availability solved.
Default to Simple routing for a rollout or location-aware requirement because it sounds safest.
Assume a fast, globally cached response means the origin behind it is protected too.

scenes.narration: Here's why both instincts fail, precisely. A CloudFront distribution with one origin and no failover configured will keep serving cached content for a while during an outage — but the moment a cache entry's T T L expires, or a request needs to reach an uncacheable path, CloudFront has nowhere else to go, and the request fails exactly like it would with no C D N at all. Real origin resilience needs an explicit origin group: a primary and a secondary origin, with automatic retry on failure. And Simple routing has no health-check concept whatsoever — it returns its configured record unconditionally, forever, even if the only server behind it is dead.

props.heading: Caching delays an outage; it doesn't prevent one
steps: Cached content survives an outage only until its TTL expires or a request is uncacheable
Past that point, a cache miss with no secondary origin fails exactly like no CDN at all
Real resilience needs an explicit origin group — primary + secondary, with automatic retry
Simple routing has zero health-check concept — it returns its record unconditionally, forever
Failover, Weighted, and Latency-based routing exist precisely because Simple structurally can't

scenes.narration: Six policies, six distinct jobs. Simple: one static answer, no health awareness, no health check possible. Weighted: a proportional, adjustable traffic split — the standard tool for a canary rollout — health check optional but recommended. Latency-based: routes to whichever region is fastest for that resolver, also with an optional health check. Failover: an explicit primary and secondary, and this is the one policy where a health check isn't optional — without it attached to the primary, nothing ever switches automatically. Geolocation: routes, or restricts, by the user's geographic location, the standard fit for licensing and compliance. And Multivalue answer: several healthy I P addresses returned at once, letting the client pick — lightweight load balancing without standing up an actual load balancer.

props.heading: Route 53's six routing policies, one real behavior each

rows.label: Weighted
cells: Proportional, adjustable traffic split — canary rollouts

rows.label: Latency-based
cells: Routes to the resolver's fastest measured region

rows.label: Geolocation
cells: Routes or restricts by user's geography — compliance

rows.label: Multivalue answer
cells: Several healthy IPs returned — lightweight LB

scenes.narration: The other half of this chapter is CloudFront's origin model, and the security detail attached to each origin type. An S3 bucket serving static assets should sit behind Origin Access Control, so the bucket itself stays fully private and only that one distribution can read it. An application load balancer serves dynamic content from E C2 or Fargate, and its security group should be scoped to CloudFront's traffic where that's required. And a custom H T T P origin — something on-premises or a third-party endpoint outside AWS entirely — puts the responsibility for correct T L S configuration on you. Two more real levers worth knowing: signed U R Ls and signed cookies restrict access to cached content without touching S3 permissions at all, and versioned object keys beat broad cache invalidation as the standard, cheaper way to handle content that changes on every deploy.

props.heading: CloudFront's origin types, and the OAC detail that matters
bullets: S3 bucket — Origin Access Control keeps the bucket private; only this distribution can read it.
Application Load Balancer — dynamic content from EC2/Fargate; scope the ALB's security group to CloudFront.
Custom HTTP origin — on-prem or third-party endpoint; TLS to the origin is your responsibility.
Signed URLs and signed cookies restrict cached content without ever touching S3 permissions.
Versioned object keys beat repeated invalidation for anything that changes on every deploy.

scenes.narration: This is the table that resolves most of this chapter's scenario questions. Need the lowest latency across regions with nothing else going on — Latency-based. Need a controllable, gradual traffic shift for a rollout or a migration cutover — Weighted, and it's reversible instantly by setting a weight back to zero. Need automatic failover to a standby with zero manual intervention — Failover, and only Failover requires that health check to mean anything at all. Need to restrict or route by a user's country for compliance or licensing — Geolocation, and note that's a different job from CloudFront's own geo-restriction, which decides what content is allowed rather than which endpoint answers.

props.heading: Match the stated requirement, not the policy name

rows.label: Several healthy IPs, client picks one

scenes.narration: Three commands map to three decisions this chapter keeps testing. Creating a health check with an H T T P S path and a request interval is the piece that makes Failover routing mean anything at all — without it, a primary and secondary record are just two disconnected records. Creating an Origin Access Control, then referencing its I D in a CloudFront distribution's origin config, is how the bucket stays fully private while the distribution alone can read it. And an invalidation call clears specific cached paths after a deploy — useful occasionally, but the expensive, blunt tool compared to just versioning your object keys.

props.heading: The health check, the OAC, and the blunt tool

output: # reference this Id in the distribution's origin config; update the bucket policy to match
# for anything deployed frequently, prefer versioned keys like app.abc123.js instead

scenes.narration: Take a concrete case. A streaming company must ensure its EU-based users see only EU-licensed catalog content, and separately wants those same users routed to the lowest-latency endpoint available. The trap answer reaches for one feature and assumes it does both jobs — usually Route 53 geolocation routing alone. Worked through the framework properly: Route 53's routing, whether geolocation or latency-based, decides which regional endpoint answers the query. CloudFront's own geo-restriction, configured independently on the distribution, decides what content that endpoint is allowed to serve at all. Both are needed, deliberately combined — picking only one leaves the other requirement unmet.

props.heading: A streaming platform's EU licensing requirement

profile.verdict: Combine Route 53 latency-based or geolocation routing (which endpoint answers) with CloudFront geo-restriction (what content that endpoint serves) — one feature alone leaves half the requirement unmet.

scenes.narration: Try these yourselves before we reveal the answers. First: a team configures two records under Simple routing, expecting automatic failover if one server goes down — and it never happens. Why not? Second: a company wants to shift roughly fifteen percent of production traffic to a new version, adjustable without a redeploy, and be able to reverse it instantly. Which policy, and what's the actual mechanism?

questions.prompt: A team configures two Route 53 records under Simple routing, expecting automatic failover if one becomes unreachable. It never happens. Why?
options: Simple routing has no health-check concept at all — it returns the configured record unconditionally regardless of endpoint health
Simple routing only checks health once every 24 hours by default
Two records under Simple routing silently merge into a Multivalue answer set
Failover requires CloudFront to be in front of both records first

questions.prompt: A company wants to shift about 15% of production traffic to a new version, adjustable live without a redeploy, and reversible instantly. Which routing policy fits, and how?
options: Latency-based routing, since it already load-balances across multiple healthy endpoints
Weighted routing — two records with proportional weights (e.g. 85/15), adjustable by updating the weights alone, reversible by setting a weight back to 0
Failover routing, using the new version as the SECONDARY record
Multivalue answer routing, since it can return more than one IP address per query

scenes.narration: Here's why. Simple routing structurally cannot fail over — it has zero health-check awareness, so it keeps confidently returning a dead server's address forever, no matter how many records are configured. And the traffic-shift question is Weighted routing's exact use case: two records carrying old and new versions get proportional weights, Route 53 splits queries accordingly, and the split changes live by editing the weights alone — no application code, and no redeploy, on either side.

answers.prompt: Why didn't Simple routing fail over automatically?
answers.correct: Simple routing has no health-check concept at all — it returns its configured record unconditionally.
answers.rationale: No number of records under Simple routing changes this — it is structurally incapable of health awareness. Automatic failover specifically requires Failover routing with a health check attached to the primary record.

answers.prompt: Which policy shifts 15% of traffic, adjustable live and reversible instantly?
answers.correct: Weighted routing — proportional weights on two records, changed live, reset to zero to fully reverse.
answers.rationale: Weighted routing distributes traffic across records in proportion to their configured weights. Changing the weights alone shifts the split with no deployment and no code change — exactly the mechanism behind canary rollouts and gradual migration cutovers.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. Caching is not failover — surviving an origin outage needs an explicit origin group with origin failover, configured on purpose. Simple routing cannot fail over, full stop, because it has no health-check concept at all. CloudFront's geo-restriction and Route 53's geolocation routing are different features answering different questions — one decides what content is allowed, the other decides which endpoint answers — and a scenario needing both compliance and performance needs both, deliberately combined. Origin Access Control, never a public bucket, is the correct way for CloudFront to reach private S3. And versioned object keys beat broad invalidation for anything that changes on every deploy. Next up: chapter thirteen goes deep on resilience and disaster recovery — the two numbers, R T O and R P O, that drive every D R decision, the four real strategy tiers from backup-and-restore to active-active, and why Multi-A Z and multi-region protect against two genuinely different failure scenarios.

props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: Caching is not failover — surviving an origin outage needs an explicit origin group with origin failover.
Simple routing cannot fail over at all — it has zero health-check concept, by design.
Only Failover routing requires a health check; Weighted, Latency-based, and Multivalue support one optionally.
CloudFront geo-restriction (what content) and Route 53 geolocation (which endpoint) are different jobs, often needed together.
OAC keeps an S3 origin private; versioned object keys beat broad invalidation for content that changes on every deploy.
